why: Scope drift is visible only by reading a session's own transcript and comparing it to the original prompt; the briefing says no harness gives a cross-session view and none flags anything about how work relates to intent. git status shows changed files (one command) but not whether they were in scope, so the real work is correlating prompt against edits across several panes.

Read as an action: answering a blocked prompt today means finding the pane and typing. The briefing says a session's own state is fully visible in its own terminal, so the answer surface already exists; the cost is only locating the tab among 3-12 panes. Removing the trip is convenience, not loss prevention, since the blocked-state detection is the part that actually unblocks work.

Component parts are cheap on Claude (/usage, Barista status line) and Codex (native usage line), but the briefing says quota is shown as a current figure only, is absent on most harnesses, and no harness projects burn forward. A single go/no-go therefore means visiting several places and doing the projection by hand. Assumed the cross-harness case: mixed Claude plus non-quota harnesses.

Explicit split assumed: the eight non-Claude harnesses. Each shows only its own session and the briefing says none surfaces anything about other sessions and no harness delivers notification off the machine. Detection means cycling panes or tmux capture-pane repeatedly over time, which is exactly the correlate-across-time pattern a normal user will not sustain. An agent sitting at an unanswered prompt is dead time, so instant knowledge prevents concrete waste.

The briefing states flatly that no harness estimates how long the current turn will take, so a single come-back time across sessions has no native input at all and cannot be assembled by hand except by guessing. Impact is real and recurring - it converts polling into leaving the desk - but it changes scheduling rather than preventing outright loss.

Reachable but manual: the briefing offers tmux list-panes to enumerate panes and git status inside a repo, so a competent user could infer two sessions sharing a working tree, but nothing native correlates session to repo and no harness shows other sessions. Most users discover the collision after the fact, in a conflicted or clobbered diff, which is concrete lost work.

The briefing is direct: no harness retains queryable history across sessions about what the user did or how often they were interrupted. Reconstructing an attention ledger by hand from scattered session files is effectively unobtainable. But the outcome named is making a case for delegating - retrospective and occasional, not a decision the user faces regularly.

A finished session is fully visible in its own pane, so the raw fact is one glance away if you look; what is missing is knowing you never came back. That is a correlation over time across panes, and the briefing says no harness keeps cross-session history and none shows other sessions. Impact is collecting output already paid for - recurring waste rather than catastrophe.

The briefing does not cover any notion of task stake or consequence on any harness, so I am reasoning from first principles: the user wrote the prompts, so the information partly lives in their head, and recovering it means re-reading each session prompt across many panes. Sorting by consequence is a genuine triage improvement but mostly reorders work the user would get to anyway. Low confidence - not covered by the briefing.

The briefing names the command directly: Claude Code has /usage reporting quota, and Barista caches 5-hour percentage plus reset time locally so users running it see it unprompted on the status line. That is one command or already on screen. Assumed the Claude case, since 5-hour windows are a Claude construct; on harnesses without quota display this signal has no native source. Avoiding a force-pause mid-task is concrete loss prevention.
